ImageDescription.value: When Charles M. Robinson designed the dormitories of Old Campus at the College of William & Mary, he connected each building with an arcaded pathway he dubbed "cloisters". The cloister depicted here connects Barrett Hall (right) with Chandler Hall. McGlothin-Street Hall, an academic hall along the Sunken Garden, is visible in the background in the center-left.

ImageDescription.value:
Shops on Duke of Gloucester Street., Postcard

Colonial Williamsburg is a group of buildings populated with historical reenactors who demonstrate aspects of colonial daily life.

Starting in 1926, with the financial backing of John D. Rockefeller Jr., Colonial Williamsburg was re-constructed from a living town whose inhabitants and post-Colonial-era buildings were removed.

-- Wikipedia

ImageDescription.value:
Willliamsburg was the capital of Virginia as a British Colony from 1699 to 1780,  The capital was moved to Richmond for greater safety during the Revolutionary war since then.  Much of the colonial city of Williamsburg deteriorated in later years.  It was rebuilt and restored as Colonial Williamsburg, from 1926 through the 1930s.  Most of the money was provided by John D. Rockefeller Jr., the son of the founder of the Standard Oil Co.
The Governor's Palace was originally built in 1705-1721.  It was destroyed by fire in 1781.  It was rebuilt in the reconstruction and opened in 1934.

ImageDescription.value: Presentation copy of the Statutes of the Order of the Garter for Prince William, Duke of Gloucester. Gloucester was knighted in 1696 at age 7. This manuscript was gifted to the College of William & Mary in Virginia in 1957 by Elizabeth II during her visit to Williamsburg. This image was taken in the Earl Gregg Swem Library, where it was on display in commemoration of Elizabeth following her passing.

ImageDescription.value: A photograph of one of the rooms in the restored Williamsburg Beay School at Colonial Williamsburg in August 2025. The darker wood floorboards towards wall with the window are original to the 18th-century construction of the building, with the lighter floorboards added during the restoration. The furnishings and walls are not original, with some modern materials used in places to prevent stress to the structure.

ImageDescription.value: Willliamsburg was the capital of Virginia as a British Colony from 1699 to 1780,  The capital was moved to Richmond during the Revolutionary War.  Much of the colonial city of Williamsburg deteriorated in later years.  It was rebuilt and restored as Colonial Williamsburg, from 1926 through the 1930s.  The Governor's Palace was originally built in 1705-1721.  It was destroyed by fire in 1781.  It was rebuilt in the reconstruction and opened in 1934.

ImageDescription.value: Bruton Parish was established in Williamsburg (then called Middle Plantation) in 1674.  The current church building was built in 1711-1715.  It is an Anglican (Episcopalian) church.  It is part of Colonial Williamsburg, but is the original building, not a reconstruction.

ImageDescription.value:
A building believed to be the oldest surviving schoolhouse for Black children in the U.S. was hoisted onto a flatbed truck and moved a half-mile Friday into Colonial Williamsburg, a Virginia museum that continues to expand its emphasis on African American history.

Built 25 years before the American Revolution, the original structure stood near the college campus of William & Mary. The two-story pinewood building held as many as 30 students at a time, some of them free Black children studying alongside the enslaved.

Hundreds of people lined the streets to celebrate its slow-speed trip into the heart of the living history museum, which tells the story of Virginia’s colonial capital through interpreters and restored buildings.

Artist.value: Richard Ricciardi

ImageDescription.value: Picture depicts the Wren Chapel of the Sir Christopher Wren Building on the Historic Campus of the College of William & Mary. As with the other buildings on Historic Campus, the Wren Building was restored by the Colonial Williamsburg project in the 1920s—1930s. The chapel's appearance is based on designs by Wren but shares very little materially with its pre-restoration renditions. The Wren Cross, which was donated by Bruton Parish and was the subject of controversy following its removal from the altar in 2006, is visible in its display case on the left.
